author: dgusakov
content:
We do! But the complication is not figuring out the code fix. This is doable, and thanks for proving it!

The issue is the audit, release, future maintenance, and off-chain parts. In practice, it is cheaper for Lido to do nothing and be ready to pull the brakes should we see at least 1 case.

The idea was to improve the way we do this one-time thing (which is already very "interestingly" done) in a safe way for all protocols rather than creating patches on the app side.

Anyway. Thanks for the PR!

author: nflaig
content: so the alternative is to not allow deposits for ~21 days I suppose?

author: nflaig
content: so the reason why this was not changed when we did EIP-8282 was because we wanted to have minimal changes, it was already late in the process, but indeed it would have been safe since we allow the same pubkey to exist for both a builder and validator

author: nflaig
content: and to be honest it's still not clear from first principles what the right way to do it from a protocol/spec perspective, but of course if you bring staking pools into the picture it's clear that we should adopt https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5736 as I don't see a major downside to it (at least right now) but it seems way too late now to do this, we did all the deposit attacks and testing on devnet-8 already, maybe you know because I killed 3 clients there 😄 but I really don't think it's safe to change code paths here now as we already even cut our hoodi release, and testing surface would be too little imo

author: george_avs
content:
For Lido, we see two options:
- Keep deposits running, monitor, and handle recovery if an exploit occurs  (which is unlikely)
- Pause new deposits ahead of the fork

And the first option currently seems more reasonable for us. Other protocols may have different options, but i believe deposit pause should work for all delegated staking protocols

And other applications that rely on deposit processing might also be affected (but that's more a matter of being careful in assessment, I don't know of any good examples)

author: nflaig
content: the deposit front running I can see why someone would do this but I don't see why anyone would send a builder deposit followed by a validator deposit for same pubkey otherwise, it would still be good to understand if this has any real impact if it happens

author: george_avs
content:
One possible reason is just to grief protocols that use a 1 eth predeposit and have protection against front-running.

Depending on the protocol, the attack could cost the operator little or nothing if there’s no extra penalty. I don’t see an obvious incentive to do it, but it could just be griefing.

They could still mess with the protocol’s accounting or leave funds stuck if the usual recovery path needs a validator proof. So the goal could simply be to cause trouble, even without making money.

Or it could simply be an operational mistake, though that seems unlikely.
